turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Thanks for joining. I'm Priya, I lead the platform team. This is a technical screen, so I'll ask about your background and then we'll dig into a design problem. Sound good?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Sounds great. For background, I've spent the last four years on backend systems, mostly Node and Postgres, with a stretch owning our job-processing pipeline.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: The job pipeline is a good place to start. What did that system do, and what was the hardest part of running it?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: It processed webhook events into downstream syncs. The hardest part was exactly-once delivery — we kept getting duplicate side effects when workers crashed mid-job.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: How did you handle that? Walk me through the mechanism.

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: We made the workers idempotent and used a claim with a lease. A worker would claim a row, and if it died, a reaper requeued the job after the lease expired.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: That's a solid pattern. Let me pin one thing: how did you pick the lease length?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Honestly, we set it to five minutes and mostly left it. I don't think we ever tuned it against the actual worst-case job time, which in hindsight was a gap.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Fair and honest. Let's switch to design. Suppose you had to build a queue on Postgres from scratch — no Redis, no SQS. How would you claim jobs safely across many workers?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: I'd use SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED inside an UPDATE, so each worker atomically grabs a different unlocked row. That avoids two workers claiming the same job.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Good. Now how do you keep the claim query fast when the table has millions of completed rows?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: A partial index on the queued rows only, so the planner isn't scanning completed history. You index where status equals queued, ordered by run-at.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Nice. One more: how would you add observability so you know when jobs are backing up?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: Um, I'd probably log completions and errors. Beyond that I haven't done much with metrics dashboards, so I'd lean on whatever the team already uses.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: That's useful to know. Observability is an area we'd want to grow with you. What questions do you have for me?

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: What does the on-call rotation look like, and how much of the roadmap is greenfield versus maintaining existing systems?

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: On-call is one week in six, and right now it's roughly sixty-forty greenfield to maintenance. I'll follow up on the exact rotation after this.

turns.speaker: Candidate
turns.text: That's helpful, thank you. I'm genuinely interested in the queue and pipeline work you described.

turns.speaker: Priya
turns.text: Great. Thanks for walking through all of that. We'll be in touch on next steps.
